title: Quarto draft — preview notes
text:
This is a draft Quarto build of the portfolio, living alongside the existing Jekyll site so nothing breaks while we iterate.


From inside this folder:
cd quarto
quarto preview
That’ll open it at http://localhost:<port> and live-reload as files change. Quit with Ctrl-C.
If you don’t have Quarto installed yet:
brew install --cask quarto




index.qmd — homepage. Hero karyotype, tagline, three “what I do” lines, three featured work cards, footer.
about.qmd — the real story. Short version, “why now,” what I bring, lived-experience note.
work/index.qmd — samples landing.
samples/*.qmd — your three existing genomics samples, ported.
assets/karyotype.svg — the hero. A stylized 23-pair karyotype I drew in SVG. Swap it for a real spectral-karyotype image when we find or commission one — just replace the file at the same path.
assets/headshot.jpg — copied from the Escaping academia folder.
styles.scss — palette, typography, layout. All the visual decisions live here.
_quarto.yml — site config (navbar, theme, etc.).





Voice on home + about. Does it sound like you? If any sentence makes you cringe, mark it.
Karyotype. It’s drawn — not a real photographic SKY karyotype. Easy to swap. Tell me if the proportions/colors feel right or if you’d rather have a real one (I can recommend sources).
The three “what I do” lines. Do they cover what you actually do, in your words?
The featured work order. Patient → clinician → review memo. Reasonable?
Headshot. Currently round, 220px, in the about page. Want it on the homepage too?
Lived-experience paragraph on the About page. Lean-in version is in there. Tone okay? Too much, not enough, just right?





Sample pages still look default-Quarto on the inside; we’ll style them once you bless the homepage direction.
The Safe Evolution and teaching-design samples mentioned on the work page — we’ll write those as new pieces.
Domain / deployment. Once you bless this, we promote quarto/ to be the root of the site (or move the Jekyll files into _legacy/) and update GitHub Pages settings.
A real karyotype image (if you want one).

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Internal Review Memo (Anonymized Example)
Author: Jodie Wiggins, Ph.D.
Role Context: Scientific Director / Scientific Content Lead
Purpose: Demonstrate scientific review, risk assessment, and strategic guidance for scientific and medical communications

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Context
This memo illustrates my approach to reviewing and guiding scientific content at a leadership level. The example below reflects a representative internal scientific review, conducted to assess accuracy, interpretive risk, clarity, and alignment with audience and strategic objectives.
The focus of this review is scientific oversight rather than line editing, with emphasis on judgment, risk-aware framing, and support for high-quality, fit-for-purpose communication.

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Reviewed Content (Anonymized)

Format: 12-slide educational slide deck

Audience: Healthcare professionals and scientific stakeholders

Purpose:
To summarize current scientific understanding of a disease area, including biological mechanisms, emerging research findings, and areas of active investigation

Source Material:
Peer-reviewed literature, mechanistic studies, and clinical research

Development Context:
Content developed by a multidisciplinary team for educational use

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Summary Assessment
Overall, the content demonstrates a high level of scientific rigor, thoughtful evidence selection, and clear educational intent, reflecting strong foundational work by the team. With small, targeted refinements, the material can further reduce interpretive risk, enhance clarity for the intended audience, and strengthen alignment between the evidence presented and the resulting conclusions. These adjustments build on an already solid framework and will help ensure the content is as clear, credible, and impactful as possible.

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Strengths Identified

Scientific Accuracy and Evidence Base
The content demonstrates strong scientific rigor and careful use of evidence throughout. Key mechanistic claims are supported by appropriate primary literature, and citations are used consistently to anchor interpretations in data rather than speculation.
Representative strengths include: - Clear and accurate depiction of the biological pathway of interest, with mechanistic steps aligned with current peer-reviewed understanding.
- Effective integration of findings from multiple study types (e.g., mechanistic studies and clinical research) to provide a balanced scientific picture rather than relying on a single line of evidence.
These choices establish a solid and credible scientific foundation for the material.



Logical Organization and Narrative Flow
The content is well structured, with a logical progression from foundational concepts to more detailed scientific discussion. This sequencing supports comprehension and allows readers to build understanding as the narrative advances.
Representative strengths include: - Early introduction of core biological concepts and terminology, which are then consistently referenced and built upon in later sections.
- Use of intermediate summary slides or transitions that reinforce key takeaways before introducing additional complexity.
This organization supports clarity and reduces cognitive load for the audience.



Appropriate Educational Tone
The material maintains a clear educational focus and avoids promotional framing. Language choices consistently signal that the science is being presented to inform understanding rather than to direct conclusions or actions.
Representative strengths include: - Careful framing of emerging data as part of an evolving evidence base, rather than presenting preliminary findings as definitive.
- Explicit use of neutral, explanatory language when discussing mechanisms and research outcomes, reinforcing the educational intent of the content.
This tone supports responsible interpretation and aligns well with expectations for scientific and medical education materials.

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Strategic Recommendations
The following recommendations are intended to build on the content’s existing strengths by enhancing clarity, appropriately calibrating interpretation, and reinforcing alignment between evidence and conclusions. These are small, targeted refinements that support scientific rigor while improving usability and confidence for the intended audience.


1. Calibrate Interpretive Language to Match Evidence Strength

Why this matters
Precise calibration of interpretive language helps maintain scientific credibility and supports responsible audience understanding, particularly when presenting emerging or evolving data.

Several statements would benefit from minor wording adjustments to more explicitly reflect the current strength of evidence. This does not change the scientific message, but ensures that interpretations are consistently aligned with what the data can support.
Recommended approach: - Use language that distinguishes association from causation where appropriate
- Clearly signal when findings are hypothesis-generating or under active investigation
Example language strategies: - “Current evidence suggests…”
- “Has been associated with…”
- “Is an area of ongoing research…”



2. Surface Key Limitations and Uncertainty at Decision Points

Why this matters
Explicit acknowledgment of uncertainty reinforces trust and prevents overextension of conclusions, especially in educational scientific content.

While limitations are present in the underlying literature, they are not always surfaced at the points where conclusions are drawn. Briefly highlighting these considerations strengthens credibility without adding unnecessary complexity.
Recommended approach: - Incorporate concise statements addressing study design, population scope, or variability in findings
- Reinforce where evidence is converging versus where it remains incomplete
Outcome:
Improved transparency and a clearer signal to the audience about how confidently findings should be interpreted.



3. Strengthen Narrative Signposting and Message Hierarchy

Why this matters
Clear signposting helps audiences orient themselves within complex scientific material and retain key takeaways.

The overall structure is strong; however, elevating key messages earlier and reinforcing them throughout the narrative will further enhance clarity and impact.
Recommended approach: - Introduce high-level scientific takeaways early in the content
- Use brief transition statements to connect detailed sections back to overarching objectives
Outcome:
A more cohesive narrative that reinforces strategic intent while preserving scientific depth.



4. Support Accessibility Through Layered Detail

Why this matters
Layered presentation allows diverse audiences to engage with content at an appropriate depth without diluting rigor.

Some highly technical sections could benefit from brief contextual framing to support readers with varying levels of background knowledge.
Recommended approach: - Add short framing statements or summaries before dense technical sections
- Maintain detailed explanations for readers seeking deeper engagement
Outcome:
Improved usability across the intended audience while maintaining scientific precision.

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Summary
These recommendations are designed to enhance an already strong piece of scientific content. By making small, targeted refinements to language, structure, and framing, the material can further strengthen its clarity, credibility, and educational impact while remaining firmly grounded in the underlying science.

title: Scientific Content Review & Strategic Recommendations
text:
Conclusion
This review reflects my approach to scientific content leadership: balancing accuracy, clarity, and strategic intent while proactively identifying risks related to overinterpretation, ambiguity, or audience mismatch. My goal in this role is to elevate content through thoughtful guidance, support contributors in producing their strongest work, and ensure that scientific communications are credible, responsible, and fit for purpose.


Notes for Reviewers
This memo is an anonymized, representative example intended to demonstrate scientific oversight, mentorship, and strategic review at a leadership level. It is not tied to a specific product, therapeutic area, or client.

title: Understanding Clinical Exome and Genome Testing
text:
Audience: Healthcare Providers, Clinical Geneticists, Genetic Counselors
Purpose: To support accurate interpretation and responsible clinical use of exome and genome sequencing results
Context: Scientific writing sample demonstrating translation of genomic testing methodology into clinician-facing technical content



Clinical exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing (WGS) are used both to diagnose known rare genetic diseases and to evaluate patients whose conditions remain undiagnosed after standard testing. When appropriately applied and interpreted, these technologies can provide actionable insights that inform diagnosis, guide clinical management, and support patient care. However, effective use requires a clear understanding of what these tests can—and cannot—reliably determine.
This brief outlines the core capabilities, interpretive considerations, and limitations of clinical exome and genome sequencing to support informed clinical decision-making.






## What Exome and Genome Sequencing Are


Exome sequencing focuses on the protein-coding regions of the genome, where a substantial proportion of currently recognized disease-causing variants have been identified.


Whole genome sequencing (WGS) captures both coding and non-coding regions, enabling evaluation of regulatory and other non-coding variation that may contribute to disease in select cases.


Selection of testing modality should be guided by clinical context, prior testing history, and diagnostic goals.






Exome and genome sequencing can reliably detect certain classes of genetic variants, with detection scope determined by the testing modality. Exome sequencing identifies single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions and deletions (indels) within protein-coding regions, while genome sequencing enables detection of these variants across both coding and non-coding regions of the genome.
When combined with robust variant annotation, curated reference databases, and phenotype-driven analysis, sequencing results may support the identification of variants associated with genetic disease in patients with suspected inherited conditions.




Clinical laboratories classify variants using established frameworks that consider multiple lines of evidence, including population frequency data, functional studies, segregation analysis, and prior clinical observations.
Common classifications include: - Pathogenic
- Likely pathogenic
- Variant of uncertain significance (VUS)
- Likely benign
- Benign
Pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants may be considered consistent with a genetic diagnosis when they align with the patient’s clinical presentation. Variants classified as benign or likely benign are not expected to contribute to disease. Variants of uncertain significance (VUS) reflect insufficient evidence to determine whether a variant is pathogenic or benign and should not be used as the sole basis for clinical decision-making.
It is important to recognize that variant classification reflects the current state of scientific evidence and may change as new data emerge. Clinical interpretation should integrate sequencing results with patient phenotype, family history, and additional diagnostic information.




Accurate and detailed phenotypic information substantially improves variant interpretation. Phenotype-driven analysis enables prioritization of variants that are most consistent with observed clinical features, reducing ambiguity and supporting more confident conclusions.
Incomplete or nonspecific phenotype data can limit interpretive power and increase the likelihood of uncertain results.




While powerful, exome and genome sequencing have important limitations:

Not all disease-causing variants are detectable with current sequencing technologies

Structural variants, repeat expansions, and certain mosaic variants may be missed or incompletely characterized

A negative result does not exclude a genetic etiology

Variants of uncertain significance should not be used as the sole basis for clinical decision-making

Understanding these limitations is essential for setting appropriate expectations and avoiding over-interpretation.




Clinical genomic testing is most effective when used as part of a comprehensive diagnostic strategy that includes clinical evaluation, family history, and ongoing re-assessment as scientific knowledge evolves. Clear communication with patients and families regarding uncertainty, limitations, and the potential need for reinterpretation over time is critical.
Exome sequencing is often appropriate as a first-line test for suspected single-gene conditions, while genome sequencing may be considered when prior testing is negative or when broader variant detection is clinically warranted.




Exome and genome sequencing offer transformative opportunities in the diagnosis of genetic disease, but their clinical value depends on careful interpretation, appropriate contextualization, and responsible use. By understanding both the capabilities and limitations of these technologies, healthcare providers can maximize their benefit while maintaining scientific rigor and patient trust.

title: The Details
text:
Jodie Wiggins, PhD



  There is no knowledge that is not power.
  — Ralph Waldo Emerson

Making the power that is inherent in knowledge accessible is what I do.
My background is in genetics and evolutionary biology, specifically, a PhD plus over a decade of university teaching, but what I actually spend my time on is harder to categorize: designing the structures that help people understand genuinely difficult things. That might mean a flipped course that took a 39% failure rate to under 5%. Or a cross-disciplinary educator workshop that succeeded so thoroughly it surprised the people who commissioned it. Or a suite of original videos, active learning sessions, and assessment frameworks built from scratch because the existing materials weren’t good enough.
I think carefully about where people get lost and I design backward from that. I’m most useful when the problem is we have complex information and the people who need it aren’t getting it. That could be a content problem, a structure problem, or sometimes a trust problem. The core of addressing all three is curiosity.
Curiosity is my superpower.


I hold a PhD in integrative biology, working in genetics and evolutionary biology, and have over a decade of university teaching at Oklahoma State where I’m currently a Teaching Associate Professor. I also taught K–12 science for three years before that. I read the discipline-based education research literature. It is difficult to narrow down who to mention but Eyler, Ambrose et al., Blum, Theobald et al., McGuire, and Lang tend to sit at the top of the stack. I’ve continued my training in instructional design for adult learners, learning measurement, culturally responsive pedagogy (Smithsonian), open educational resources, science communication summits, and program management.
Technically, I’m fluent in R and Python — particularly for data visualization and analysis — and across the modern Markdown / Quarto / GitHub Pages publishing stack. I’ve coordinated research teams, led multi-section instructional operations at scale, and built educational programs from scratch.



I rebuilt our 8-section General Genetics course from the ground up: flipped, OER-based, evidence-driven. Three years later, the results are still holding. I’m now leveraging that to redesign our Introductory Biology course.

  
    
      39%
      →
      <5%
    
    Drop/fail/withdraw rate in General Genetics, before and after the redesign. Three consecutive years and counting.
  
  
    
      2,000+
    
    Students per year in Introductory Biology — the next course on my redesign list.
  

Adjacent to that: I co-founded our department’s Community of Practice, helped write Safe Evolution — the code of conduct for the Society for the Study of Evolution and partner societies — serve on our department’s AI Integration Team, and mentor K–8 students at Prairie Wood Forest School.
Before higher ed I was a certified K–12 science teacher. Before that I was a kid who couldn’t stop asking questions about how things worked.



After a decade in academia, I want to do this work somewhere it lives closer to where scientific information actually meets people’s lives. Medical communications. Scientific content strategy. Patient education. Editorial leadership.
Same skills, different impact.



I’ve also navigated the medical system as a complex patient — hEDS, MCAS, dysautonomia. The power of my knowledge saved my life.
I understand, from the other side of the chart, what it costs when scientific information isn't accessible to the people who need it most.
That perspective shapes how I write for patients, providers, and caregivers and the kind of work I want to do next.



Roles where the work is substantive, the team is collaborative, and the mission is real.
Full-time scientific content roles, content strategy and editorial leadership, freelance medical and patient communications — and conversations that don’t fit any of those boxes.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
section: What Are Exome and Genome Sequencing?
text:
What Are Exome and Genome Sequencing?
Exome and genome sequencing are genetic tests used that evaluate a person’s DNA in order to identify possible genetic causes of health conditions.
Your DNA contains instructions that tell your body how to grow and function. Much of what the body does is carried out by proteins, which perform essential tasks in cells and tissues. Some parts of DNA provide the instructions for making proteins, while other parts help regulate how cells function. Changes in these DNA instructions—called variants—can sometimes be associated with disease.
Exome sequencing focuses on the parts of DNA that directly code for proteins. Genome sequencing examines both these protein-coding regions and the rest of the DNA, including regions involved in regulating how cells function.
Both tests are used to help doctors better understand conditions that may have a genetic cause, especially when symptoms are unexplained or previous testing has not provided clear answers.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
section: Why Might These Tests Be Recommended?
text:
Why Might These Tests Be Recommended?
Exome and genome sequencing are often used when:

A person has symptoms that suggest a genetic condition

A diagnosis is unclear despite prior medical testing

There is concern about a condition with a possible inherited component

Understanding whether genetics may play a role could guide care or future planning

These tests can sometimes identify a genetic explanation for symptoms and help doctors confirm or refine a diagnosis.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
text:
What Can These Tests Identify?
Exome and genome sequencing can detect certain types of changes in DNA, including small changes that affect individual genes.
Depending on the type of test used:

Exome sequencing looks for changes in genes that directly code for proteins

Genome sequencing looks for similar changes across the entire DNA sequence, including regions outside genes

When combined with detailed medical information and family history, these results may help identify genetic changes that are relevant to a person’s health.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
text:
Understanding Genetic Test Results
Genetic test results are typically placed into categories based on the available scientific evidence.
Some results may:

Support a genetic explanation for a person’s condition

Indicate a change in DNA that is not expected to affect health

Identify a change where there is not enough information yet to know whether it is related to disease

A result called a Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) means that scientists do not currently have enough evidence to determine whether a specific DNA change is related to a health condition. These findings are common and do not confirm or rule out a diagnosis on their own.

Important: A Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) does not confirm or rule out a diagnosis and should not be used on its own to make medical decisions.

Importantly, genetic test results may be updated over time as new research becomes available.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
section: Why Results Don’t Always Provide Clear Answers
text:
Why Results Don’t Always Provide Clear Answers

Note: A negative result does not mean symptoms are not real or important. It may mean the genetic cause is not yet identifiable with current knowledge.

Even with advanced testing, genetic results do not always explain a person’s symptoms.
This can happen because:

Not all genetic causes of disease are currently known

Some types of genetic changes are difficult to detect

A condition may not be genetic in origin

The genetic contribution may be complex or involve multiple factors

A negative or uncertain result does not mean that symptoms are not real or important.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
text:
Using Genetic Testing Responsibly
Genetic testing is most helpful when used as part of a broader medical evaluation. Doctors consider genetic results alongside medical history, physical findings, family history, and other tests.
Clear communication between healthcare providers, patients, and families is essential—especially when results are uncertain or may change over time.
Genetic testing is a powerful tool, but it is only one piece of the diagnostic process.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
text:
Key Takeaways

Exome and genome sequencing can help identify genetic causes of health conditions, but they do not always provide definitive answers

Results may change as science advances

Uncertain results are common and should be interpreted carefully

Genetic testing is most informative when interpreted in the context of a person’s overall medical care

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Will exome or genome sequencing always provide a diagnosis?
No. While these tests can sometimes identify genetic factors related to a person’s symptoms, they do not always lead to a clear diagnosis. Some conditions may not have a known genetic cause, and in other cases, current science may not yet be able to fully explain the findings.



What does it mean if my results are uncertain?
An uncertain result, often called a Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS), means that there is not enough scientific evidence at this time to determine whether a specific genetic change is related to a health condition. These results are common and should not be used on their own to make medical decisions.



Can genetic test results change over time?
Yes. As scientific knowledge advances and more data become available, genetic test results may be updated or reinterpreted. A result that is uncertain today may be better understood in the future.



Does a negative result mean there is no genetic explanation?
Not necessarily. A negative result means that the test did not identify a genetic finding that clearly explains the condition at this time. It does not rule out a genetic contribution, and it does not mean that symptoms are not real or important.



Why might genome sequencing be recommended instead of exome sequencing?
Genome sequencing examines a broader portion of DNA than exome sequencing. It may be considered when prior testing has not provided clear answers or when a broader evaluation of genetic variation is clinically appropriate. The choice of test depends on individual circumstances and clinical judgment.



Who can help me understand my results?
Healthcare providers and genetic counselors are trained to explain genetic test results and discuss what they may mean for you and your family. They can also help address questions, uncertainty, and next steps.

title: For Patients: Understanding Exome and Genome Sequencing
section: What to Ask Your Healthcare Provider
text:
What to Ask Your Healthcare Provider

Tip: Genetic testing is most informative when interpreted in the context of medical history, symptoms, and family history.

If you are considering exome or genome sequencing, or if you have already received results, the following questions may help guide conversations with your healthcare provider or genetic counselor:

What is the goal of this test for my specific situation?
Why is exome or genome sequencing being recommended instead of other tests?
What types of results are most likely, and what would they mean for my care?
What are the possible limitations of this test?
How should uncertain results be interpreted?
Could my results change over time as new information becomes available?
How might these results affect my medical care, screening, or future planning?
Are there implications for my family members?
What follow-up or additional testing, if any, might be recommended?
Who should I contact if I have questions about my results in the future?

These discussions can help ensure that genetic testing is used thoughtfully and that results are understood within the context of your overall medical care.

title: Building an education program from nothing
text:
Program design & launch · Federally-funded research initiative
    Building an education program from nothing
    An education and outreach division for a federally-funded phylogenetics initiative — including a researcher-educator workshop model whose results surprised the people who commissioned it.
    
      Program design and launch
      Cross-functional team leadership
      Workshop facilitation
      Instructional technology development
      Stakeholder management
    
  

  
    The problem
    A federally-funded phylogenetics research initiative had no education or outreach component. The science was significant and publicly funded, but inaccessible to educators and the broader public. No one on the team had built this kind of program before.
  

  
    What I did
    I created the vision, strategy, and structure for an education division from scratch. I built and coordinated a distributed cross-functional team — computer scientists, phylogenetics researchers, and educators across multiple institutions — and developed interactive web-based phylogenetic learning tools in R, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
    The centerpiece was the inaugural subject-specialist/educator collaborative workshop: a model that brought researchers and teachers together to co-produce educational resources from large-scale biological datasets. Designing the workshop meant designing the structure that would let two professional cultures actually do work together — rather than presenting at one another.
  

  
    The outcome

    
      
        
          100%
        
        Positive participant feedback from the inaugural researcher-educator workshop.
      
      
        
          < 1 yr
        
        From scoping to a launched program division, with a working workshop model and a published OER suite.
      
    

    The workshop produced a suite of open educational resources that are still publicly available. Organizers described the outcome as unlike anything they had seen before — the model demonstrated that researchers and educators could productively co-create in a structured collaborative format, a result that surprised the broader team.
  

  
    What I built

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Workshop deliverable hub
        phyloEd
        The site I built to host every educational resource produced by the workshop — interactive learning websites, full lesson plans aligned to NGSS, and teacher-facing quick-start guides. Co-developed with public-school teachers and phylogenetics researchers.
        jwiggi18.github.io/phyloEd ↗
      
    

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Flagship interactive build
        History of Earth
        An interactive learning module connecting geologic time, climate change, and biological evolution — co-developed with researchers Brian O'Meara, Dave Bapst, and Luna Sanchez Reyes alongside public-school teachers Nellie Johnson, Kellee Shuttleworth, and Cara Stephens. Maps to multiple NGSS standards across middle and high school.
        historyofearth.net ↗
      
    

    
      
        
      
      
        Parent project · NSF-funded research initiative
        Phylotastic
        The parent research initiative — a multi-institution NSF-funded effort to make the Tree of Life computable, citable, and ready-to-use. I built the education and outreach division, contributed code and R packages to the broader infrastructure, and wired up API access for the educator-facing tools.
        phylotastic.org ↗
      
    

    Source code for the phyloEd hub lives at github.com/jwiggi18/phyloEd. Phylotastic's open-source code, including R packages and API services, is at github.com/phylotastic.

title: Redesigning a failing course
text:
Course redesign · Higher education
    Redesigning a failing course
    A flipped, OER-based rebuild of General Genetics that took the drop/fail/withdraw rate from 39% to under 5% — and held there for three consecutive years.
    
      Instructional systems design
      Data-driven iteration
      Equity-centered design
      Open educational resources
      Program management
    
  

  
    The problem
    General Genetics at Oklahoma State had a nearly 40% drop/fail/withdraw rate. Students were failing in large numbers, the course relied on an expensive commercial textbook, and assessment was high-stakes exam-dependent — a structure the discipline-based education research literature consistently shows disadvantages underrepresented students.
  

  
    What I did
    I redesigned the course from the ground up using evidence from the learning sciences. I built a complete asynchronous content library — original short-form video lectures, embedded formative assessment questions, and open educational resources — that replaced the commercial textbook entirely. Weekly active-learning sessions targeted the specific conceptual bottlenecks where students consistently got lost: ploidy, meiosis, gene regulation.
    Assessment moved from high-stakes exams to mastery-based: two-attempt quizzes, homework revision opportunities, and synthesis reflections. Across eight concurrent sections, structured TA mentorship kept delivery consistent.
  

  
    The outcome

    
      
        
          39%
          →
          <5%
        
        Drop/fail/withdraw rate before and after the redesign — sustained over three consecutive years.
      
      
        
          200+
        
        Students per semester, across 8 concurrent sections, with a fully original content library.
      
    

    The redesign was recognized with an Oklahoma Regents for Higher Education OER Grant, and students nominated the course for the Arts & Sciences Distinguished Teacher Award in consecutive years.

    This was one of the most well thought out courses I have ever taken.

    I now have a new standard for which my future classes should be like.
  

  
    What I built

    
      
        
      
      
        Live website · Interactive syllabus
        Interactive General Genetics syllabus
        A student-facing syllabus built so students can find what they actually need — what to do each week, where to do it, what gets graded — without parsing a 12-page PDF. Includes expectations, accommodations, assessment policy, and instructional team.

        A growing open-access companion library that replaces the commercial textbook — units on genomes, chromosomes, ploidy, prions, and more, written from scratch and freely usable by other instructors. Built in Quarto with downloadable PDFs alongside the web version.
